added_claim_errors: "at most $660 of 2025 funds can move into 2026": wrong plan year; the user's plan year ends Dec 31, 2026, and the 2026-to-2027 carryover cap is $680 (Rev. Proc. 2025-32)
"you can incur expenses through March 15, 2026": wrong year (latest is March 15, 2027), and it is stated as a fixed date when March 15 is only the maximum a plan may set

"at most $660 of your $1,900 survives... The March dental work does not get to spend the other $1,240": wrong under the grace-period branch, where the whole balance can pay for work done by the grace end. It also contradicts B's own later sentence, and the $1,240 comes from the wrong cap (it should be $1,220)
"$1,900 becomes $0 on January 1": loosely stated. Expenses must be incurred by Dec 31, but forfeiture is measured at the end of the run-out period. Minor

reasons: Both answers correct the rollover premise at the start, tell the person to check with the plan, warn against prepaying for March work, and list sensible spend-down items. Neither mentions the 2027 open-enrollment election. A gets the 2026 figures right: a $680 carryover cap, $1,220 to spend by Dec 31, and a grace period of up to March 15. It also gives a formula that works for a lower plan cap. B anchors everything to the wrong plan year: a $660 cap for 2025 funds and a grace period ending March 15, 2026. It then says the March dental work cannot use the other $1,240, which is false if the plan has a grace period and contradicts B's own later advice. A is longer but accurate throughout, so it wins clearly.
